prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- The United Nations has sent police and military patrols to a camp in western Sudan after reports fighting there killed civilians, a U.N. spokesman said Tuesday. A file photo of refugees queuing for food in the Kalma camp in western Sudan. Aid groups have started evacuating wounded from the Kalma camp, home to 80,000 internally displaced people in the Darfur region of western Sudan. The U.N. said it received reports that Sudanese police vehicles surrounded the camp and that civilians were killed Monday during subsequent attacks inside the camp. The U.N. African Union Mission in Darfur "is extremely concerned by this serious incident [and the] circumstances will be investigated," the mission said in a statement. "It is closely monitoring the situation and [calls] on all parties to exercise restraint." A spokesman for the mission, Noureddine Nezni, said Tuesday the Dutch wing of Medecins Sans Frontieres had evacuated 47 wounded people who were being treated at a nearby hospital. Some of them -- mostly young men -- refused to be evacuated for fear of being arrested for having participated in the fighting, Nezni said. Nezni would not say how many people were killed in the Monday attacks. "There are many figures being thrown around and we hesitate to give any numbers before we are sure," he said. "We are still checking and hopefully we will have the correct figure late today." The Sudanese government said it entered the camp to look for "huge quantities of arms and criminals," Nezni said. The U.N. African Union Mission in Darfur said it sent police and military patrols to Kalma to confirm the details of the incident and provide assistance. Nezni added that the mission and some aid groups were in talks with refugees at the camp to find a lasting solution to the problems. Fighting has displaced more than two million Sudanese -- and more than 238,000 refugees live in camps across the border in eastern Chad, the U.N. says. They have been displaced by fighting that broke out in 2003, when rebels began an uprising in Darfur and the government launched a brutal counter-insurgency campaign. The Sudanese authorities armed and cooperated with Arab militias that went from village to village in Darfur, killing, torturing and raping residents there, according to the U.N., Western governments and human rights organizations. The militias targeted civilian members of tribes from which the rebels draw strength. In the past five years, an estimated 300,000 people have been killed through direct combat, disease, or malnutrition, the U.N. says. Another 2.7 million people have been forced to flee their homes because of fighting among rebels, government forces, and allied Janjaweed militias. The chief prosecutor of the International Criminal Court filed genocide charges against Sudanese President Omar Hassan al-Bashir last month for the campaign of violence in Darfur. CNN's Eunice Mafundikwa contributed to this report.

outputs.L1:
(CNN) — The United Nations has deployed police and military patrols to a camp in western Sudan following reports that fighting there left civilians dead, a U.N. spokesman said Tuesday.

A file photo shows refugees queuing for food at the Kalma camp in western Sudan.

Aid groups have begun evacuating wounded people from Kalma camp, which is home to 80,000 internally displaced people in Sudan’s western Darfur region.

The United Nations said it had received reports that Sudanese police vehicles surrounded the camp and that civilians were killed Monday in subsequent attacks inside the camp.

The U.N.-African Union Mission in Darfur said in a statement that it “is extremely concerned by this serious incident [and the] circumstances will be investigated.” The mission added that it is closely monitoring the situation and called on all parties to exercise restraint.

Noureddine Nezni, a spokesman for the mission, said Tuesday that the Dutch branch of Médecins Sans Frontières had evacuated 47 wounded people who were receiving treatment at a nearby hospital. Some of the wounded — mostly young men — refused to be evacuated out of fear that they would be arrested for having taken part in the fighting, Nezni said.

Nezni declined to say how many people were killed in Monday’s attacks.

“There are many figures being thrown around and we hesitate to give any numbers before we are sure,” he said. “We are still checking and hopefully we will have the correct figure late today.”

The Sudanese government said it entered the camp to search for “huge quantities of arms and criminals,” Nezni said.

The U.N.-African Union Mission in Darfur said it had sent police and military patrols to Kalma to verify details of the incident and provide assistance. Nezni added that the mission and several aid groups were in talks with refugees at the camp in an effort to find a lasting solution to the problems there.

Fighting has displaced more than two million Sudanese, and more than 238,000 refugees are living in camps across the border in eastern Chad, according to the United Nations.

They were displaced by fighting that erupted in 2003, when rebels launched an uprising in Darfur and the government responded with a brutal counterinsurgency campaign. According to the United Nations, Western governments, and human rights organizations, Sudanese authorities armed and cooperated with Arab militias that moved from village to village in Darfur, killing, torturing, and raping residents.

The militias targeted civilian members of tribes from which the rebels drew support.

Over the past five years, an estimated 300,000 people have been killed in direct combat or have died from disease or malnutrition, the United Nations says. Another 2.7 million people have been forced to flee their homes because of fighting among rebels, government forces, and allied Janjaweed militias.

Last month, the chief prosecutor of the International Criminal Court filed genocide charges against Sudanese President Omar Hassan al-Bashir over the campaign of violence in Darfur.

CNN’s Eunice Mafundikwa contributed to this report.

(CNN) — The United Nations deployed police and military patrols to a camp in western Sudan following reports that clashes there had resulted in civilian deaths, a U.N. spokesperson said Tuesday.

A file image showed refugees waiting in line for food at Kalma camp in western Sudan. Relief organizations have begun moving injured people out of the camp, which shelters about 80,000 internally displaced people in Sudan’s Darfur region.

According to the U.N., it had received information that Sudanese police vehicles had encircled the camp and that civilians were killed Monday in attacks that followed inside the camp.

The U.N.-African Union Mission in Darfur said in a statement that it was “extremely concerned” about the serious episode and that the circumstances surrounding it would be investigated. The mission also said it was watching developments closely and urged all sides to show restraint.

Noureddine Nezni, a spokesperson for the mission, said Tuesday that the Dutch branch of Médecins Sans Frontières had transported 47 injured people who were receiving care at a nearby hospital. Nezni said some of the wounded, most of them young men, declined to leave because they feared they might be arrested over alleged involvement in the fighting.

Nezni did not provide a death toll from Monday’s attacks. He said many different numbers were circulating, and the mission was reluctant to release a figure before confirming it. He added that officials were still verifying the information and hoped to have an accurate number later that day.

Nezni said Sudan’s government claimed it had gone into the camp to search for “huge quantities of arms and criminals.”

The U.N.-African Union Mission in Darfur said it had dispatched police and military patrols to Kalma to verify what happened and to offer assistance. Nezni also said the mission, along with several aid organizations, was speaking with camp residents in an effort to reach a long-term solution to the problems there.

The U.N. says violence has uprooted more than 2 million Sudanese people, while more than 238,000 refugees are living in camps across the border in eastern Chad.

The displacement stems from fighting that began in 2003, when rebel groups launched an uprising in Darfur and the Sudanese government responded with a harsh counterinsurgency campaign.

According to the U.N., Western governments and human rights groups, Sudanese authorities armed and worked with Arab militias that moved through Darfur villages, killing, torturing and raping residents. Those militias targeted civilians from tribes that were seen as a source of support for the rebels.

Over the previous five years, the U.N. estimates that about 300,000 people died as a result of direct fighting, illness or malnutrition. A further 2.7 million people were driven from their homes by clashes involving rebels, government troops and allied Janjaweed militias.

The previous month, the chief prosecutor of the International Criminal Court filed genocide charges against Sudanese President Omar Hassan al-Bashir over the campaign of violence in Darfur.

CNN’s Eunice Mafundikwa contributed to the report.

**U.N. patrols sent to Darfur camp after reports Sudanese forces killed civilians**

**KHARTOUM, Sudan (CNN)** — United Nations police and military patrols have been sent to Kalma camp in Sudan’s Darfur region after reports that Sudanese government forces opened fire and killed civilians there, U.N. officials said.

The patrols were dispatched to assess the situation and provide a protective presence following accounts of violence at the sprawling camp, which shelters tens of thousands of people displaced by years of conflict in Darfur.

U.N. officials said they were seeking to verify reports that Sudanese security forces entered the camp and that civilians were killed and wounded in the confrontation. Details of the incident remained unclear, and casualty figures could not immediately be independently confirmed.

Kalma camp, located near Nyala in South Darfur, is one of the largest camps for internally displaced people in the region and has often been a flashpoint between residents, Sudanese authorities and armed groups.

The joint United Nations-African Union peacekeeping mission in Darfur, known as UNAMID, has police and military personnel deployed across the region, though its movements have at times been restricted by security conditions and government controls.

Darfur has been gripped by violence since 2003, when rebel groups took up arms against the Sudanese government, accusing it of marginalizing the region. The conflict triggered a humanitarian crisis and led to the displacement of millions of people. The United Nations has estimated that hundreds of thousands have died from violence, disease and hunger linked to the conflict.

Sudan’s government has repeatedly denied targeting civilians and has disputed U.N. and human rights groups’ characterizations of the conflict.

U.N. officials said the patrols around Kalma were intended to calm tensions, monitor developments and help protect civilians as investigators sought more information about what happened.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a full wire-service report on violence at the Kalma internally displaced persons camp in western Sudan, including U.N. reaction, evacuations by Médecins Sans Frontières, and background on the Darfur conflict.
counterfactuals.output:
**NYALA, Sudan (Wire report)** — Violence at the Kalma internally displaced persons camp in Sudan’s western Darfur region has left civilians dead and wounded, prompted sharp concern from the United Nations and forced Médecins Sans Frontières to evacuate staff and curtail medical operations, aid officials and witnesses said.

The unrest erupted at Kalma, one of Darfur’s largest camps for people uprooted by the region’s long-running war, near Nyala, the capital of South Darfur. Accounts from residents and aid workers described shooting inside or around the camp, panic among displaced families and a rush of wounded people seeking treatment.

Casualty figures could not be independently verified. Local sources said several people were killed and many more injured, while humanitarian officials said insecurity and restricted access made it difficult to establish a full toll.

The United Nations said it was alarmed by the violence and urged all parties to protect civilians, allow medical access and avoid further escalation. U.N. officials called for an investigation into the incident and appealed to Sudanese authorities and armed groups to respect the civilian character of displacement camps.

“The priority must be the safety of civilians and unhindered humanitarian access,” a U.N. humanitarian official said. The U.N. also warned that renewed violence in and around camps could further destabilize Darfur, where millions of people remain dependent on aid.

Médecins Sans Frontières, the medical charity also known as Doctors Without Borders, said it had evacuated staff from the Kalma area because of the deteriorating security situation. The organization said the move was necessary to protect personnel, though it warned that the evacuation would reduce medical services for thousands of displaced people.

MSF has been among the key providers of emergency medical care in Darfur’s camps, treating trauma injuries, malnutrition, infectious diseases and maternal-health emergencies. Aid workers said any suspension of services at Kalma could have immediate consequences because camp residents often have limited access to government health facilities and face security risks when moving outside the camp.

Kalma camp has long been a flashpoint in Darfur. Established during the height of the conflict, it grew into one of the region’s most crowded and politically sensitive displacement sites, hosting tens of thousands of people who fled attacks on villages across Darfur. Sudanese authorities have at times accused armed opposition sympathizers of operating inside camps, while camp leaders and rights groups have accused government forces and allied militias of intimidation and abuses.

Darfur’s conflict began in 2003 when mostly non-Arab rebel groups took up arms against the Sudanese government, accusing Khartoum of political and economic marginalization. The government responded with a counterinsurgency campaign conducted by the army and allied Arab militias, widely known as the Janjaweed.

The fighting, scorched-earth attacks and mass displacement produced one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. The United Nations has estimated that about 300,000 people died from violence, disease and hunger linked to the conflict, while more than 2 million were displaced. Sudanese governments have disputed some international casualty estimates.

The International Criminal Court later charged former Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir and other officials with crimes including genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity over the Darfur campaign. Bashir denied the allegations.

Although large-scale fighting declined after the peak years of the war, Darfur has remained unstable. Disputes over land, militia activity, rebel-government clashes and intercommunal violence have continued to drive displacement. The withdrawal of international peacekeepers and Sudan’s broader political turmoil have added to fears among civilians in camps such as Kalma.

Humanitarian agencies say displaced people remain vulnerable to attacks, arbitrary arrest, sexual violence and limits on freedom of movement. Aid groups have repeatedly warned that insecurity, bureaucratic restrictions and funding shortages have weakened the relief response.

Following the latest violence, U.N. agencies and non-governmental organizations were assessing whether they could safely resume operations in and around Kalma. Aid officials said emergency medical care, water supplies, sanitation and food distribution were among the most urgent needs.

Residents of the camp said many families were too frightened to leave their shelters, while others searched for missing relatives. Community leaders appealed for international protection and demanded guarantees that security forces would not enter the camp without coordination with humanitarian agencies.

Sudanese officials did not immediately provide a detailed public account of the incident. In previous confrontations at displacement camps, authorities have said security operations were aimed at restoring order or pursuing criminal suspects. Rights groups have frequently disputed those accounts, saying civilians have borne the brunt of force.

The U.N. said it was continuing to monitor the situation and was in contact with local authorities, humanitarian partners and community representatives.

“Kalma’s residents have already endured years of conflict and displacement,” a humanitarian worker said. “Any interruption to medical care or aid delivery puts an already fragile population at even greater risk.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.output:
## Civilians Reported Killed in Darfur’s Kalma Camp as U.N. Urges Restraint

Civilians were reportedly killed and others wounded during a violent incident at Kalma camp, one of Darfur’s largest settlements for displaced people, prompting the evacuation of injured residents and renewed calls from the United Nations for restraint by all parties.

Kalma camp, near Nyala in South Darfur, has long sheltered tens of thousands of people uprooted by the conflict that has devastated the region since 2003. The camp has frequently been a flashpoint between displaced residents, Sudanese authorities, armed groups and peacekeepers, reflecting the broader insecurity that has persisted across Darfur for years.

According to reports from the area, violence broke out in or around the camp, leaving civilians dead and several others wounded. Injured people were evacuated for medical treatment, while humanitarian workers and international officials expressed concern about the safety of camp residents and the possibility of further escalation.

The United Nations called on all sides to exercise maximum restraint and to protect civilians, emphasizing that displaced people must not be drawn into violence or subjected to reprisals. U.N. officials have repeatedly warned that attacks in and around camps for internally displaced people can worsen an already fragile humanitarian situation, limiting access to food, medicine and other essential assistance.

The incident comes against the backdrop of Darfur’s long-running conflict, which began when rebel groups took up arms against the Sudanese government, accusing it of marginalizing the region’s non-Arab communities. Khartoum responded with a military campaign that human rights groups and U.N. investigators say was supported by allied militia forces widely known as the Janjaweed.

The Janjaweed militias were accused of carrying out widespread atrocities, including village burnings, killings, rape and forced displacement. Sudan’s government has historically denied directing the militias, though international investigators alleged that state forces and allied fighters acted together in a campaign targeting civilian populations suspected of supporting rebel groups.

The conflict led to one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, with hundreds of thousands of people estimated to have died from violence, disease and hunger, and millions displaced. Camps such as Kalma became symbols of both survival and vulnerability, housing civilians who fled attacks but remained exposed to insecurity, political pressure and restricted humanitarian access.

Darfur’s conflict also brought unprecedented international legal scrutiny. In 2009 and 2010, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir on charges including war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide related to the Darfur campaign. Bashir rejected the charges, and Sudan, which was not a party to the Rome Statute, refused to surrender him while he remained in power.

Although Bashir was ousted in 2019 after mass protests, accountability for crimes committed in Darfur remains a major unresolved issue. The ICC has continued to seek justice for victims, while survivors and rights groups have called for those responsible for atrocities to be prosecuted.

The reported killings at Kalma camp underscore the continuing volatility in Darfur and the persistent risks faced by displaced civilians. Humanitarian agencies have urged authorities and armed actors to allow medical evacuations, ensure safe access for aid workers and prevent further violence against camp residents.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

EL FASHER, Sudan (CNN) — United Nations peacekeepers have sent patrols to a camp for displaced people in western Sudan after renewed fighting raised fears for civilians already caught in Darfur’s long-running crisis, a UN spokesman said.

Noureddine Mezni, a spokesman for the UN mission in Darfur, said patrols were deployed to help calm tensions and assess conditions following clashes near the camp. He said the mission was monitoring the situation closely and working with local authorities and community leaders to prevent further violence.

The camp shelters thousands of displaced people, many of whom fled earlier waves of conflict in Darfur. Residents in such camps remain highly vulnerable, aid groups say, with limited access to food, clean water, health care and protection.

Medecins Sans Frontieres, also known as Doctors Without Borders, has repeatedly warned that insecurity in Darfur is making it harder for humanitarian workers to reach communities in need. The medical charity has said civilians displaced by fighting face growing risks from disease, malnutrition and a lack of basic services.

Darfur has been the scene of years of violence involving government forces, allied militias and rebel groups. Although international attention has fluctuated, the region remains at the center of one of Sudan’s most severe humanitarian emergencies.

Across Sudan, conflict and political instability have deepened a broader crisis, forcing millions from their homes and stretching aid operations beyond capacity. Humanitarian agencies say displaced families in Darfur are among those most at risk as renewed violence threatens to cut off already fragile lifelines.
